chapters.title: A Scandal in Bohemia
paragraphs: To Sherlock Holmes, she is always _the_ woman. I have hardly ever heard him refer to her by any other name. In his eyes she overshadows and stands above every other member of her sex. This did not mean that he felt anything resembling love for Irene Adler. His cold, precise, yet admirably balanced mind recoiled from all emotions, and from that one in particular. He was, to my mind, the most perfect machine for reasoning and observation the world had ever seen; but the role of lover would have been entirely wrong for him. He mentioned the gentler passions only to mock and sneer at them. For an observer they were admirable subjects—excellent means of uncovering the motives behind people's actions. But if a trained reasoner allowed such intrusions into his own delicate, finely adjusted nature, he would introduce a distraction that might cast doubt on every conclusion he reached. Grit in a sensitive instrument, or a crack in one of his powerful lenses, would have been no more disturbing than strong emotion in a nature like his. Yet for him there was only one woman: the late Irene Adler, of dubious and questionable reputation.

I had seen very little of Holmes recently. My marriage had gradually drawn us apart. My own complete happiness, and the domestic interests that gather around a man when he first has a home of his own, took up all my attention. Holmes, meanwhile, hated every kind of society with all his Bohemian soul. He stayed in our Baker Street lodgings, buried in his old books, passing from cocaine to ambition week by week, from the drug's drowsiness to the fierce energy of his own sharp nature. The study of crime still fascinated him as deeply as ever. He devoted his enormous intellectual gifts and extraordinary powers of observation to tracing clues and solving mysteries that the official police had given up as hopeless. Now and then I heard some indistinct report of his activities: his summons to Odessa over the Trepoff murder; his explanation of the strange tragedy of the Atkinson brothers at Trincomalee; and, finally, the mission he had carried out with such tact and success for the reigning family of Holland. Apart from these signs of his activity, which reached me along with every other reader of the daily newspapers, I knew little about my former friend and companion.

One night—the twentieth of March, 1888—I was on my way home from visiting a patient, having returned by then to civilian medical practice. My route took me through Baker Street. As I passed that familiar door, forever linked in my mind with my courtship and the dark events of the Study in Scarlet, I felt a strong desire to see Holmes again and discover how he was using his extraordinary abilities. His rooms were brightly lit. Even as I looked up, his tall, lean figure crossed the blind twice in dark silhouette. He was walking quickly and eagerly about the room, his head lowered to his chest and his hands clasped behind his back. To someone who knew every one of his moods and habits, as I did, his posture and movements told their own story. He was working again. He had emerged from his drug-induced dreams and was eagerly following the trail of some new problem. I rang the bell and was taken upstairs to the room that had once been partly my own.

He was not demonstrative. He rarely was; still, I believe he was pleased to see me. Almost without speaking, but with a friendly look, he motioned me towards an armchair, tossed me his cigar case, and pointed to a case of spirits and a gasogene in the corner. Then he stood in front of the fire and surveyed me in his peculiar, inward-looking way.
“Marriage agrees with you,” he observed. “Watson, I believe you have gained seven and a half pounds since our last meeting.”
“Seven!” I replied.
“Really? I would have said rather more. A little more, I think, Watson. And I see you are practising again. You never told me you meant to return to work.”
“How do you know, then?”
“I observe it and draw my conclusions. How do I know that you have recently been getting very wet, or that your servant girl is exceptionally clumsy and careless?”

“My dear Holmes,” I said, “this is really too much. Had you lived a few centuries earlier, they would certainly have burned you. I did take a walk in the country on Thursday and come home in a dreadful state; but I have changed my clothes, so I cannot imagine how you infer it. As for Mary Jane, she is beyond reform, and my wife has given her notice. But once again I cannot see how you arrive at that conclusion.”
He gave a quiet chuckle and rubbed his long, restless hands together.

“Nothing could be simpler,” he said. “On the inner side of your left shoe, exactly where the firelight falls, I can see six nearly parallel cuts scored into the leather. Clearly, someone made them by scraping very carelessly around the edge of the sole to get off dried mud. That gives me both conclusions: you had been out in filthy weather, and you employ a particularly vicious, boot-slashing specimen of the London maid-of-all-work. As for your medical practice, a gentleman enters my room smelling of iodoform, with a black silver-nitrate stain on his right forefinger and a bulge on the right side of his top-hat showing where he has tucked away his stethoscope. I would have to be remarkably slow not to recognise a practising member of the medical profession.”

I could not help laughing at how easily he explained his deductions. “Once you give your reasons,” I said, “it always seems so absurdly simple that I could readily do it myself. Yet every new example of your reasoning leaves me baffled until you explain how you did it. And I believe my eyes are every bit as good as yours.”

“Certainly,” he replied, lighting a cigarette and dropping into an armchair. “You look, but you do not observe. There is a clear difference. For instance, you have often seen the stairs coming up from the hall to this room.”
“Very often.”
“How many times?”
“Well, several hundred times, I suppose.”
“And how many steps are there?”
“How many steps? I couldn't say.”

“Exactly! You have seen them, yet you have not observed them. That is precisely my point. I know there are seventeen steps, because I have both seen and observed. Incidentally, since these little problems interest you, and you have been kind enough to record one or two of my minor experiences, this may interest you.” He tossed me a sheet of thick, pink-tinged notepaper that had been lying unfolded on the table. “It arrived with the last post,” he said. “Read it out.”
The note bore no date, no signature, and no address.

“There will call upon you to-night, at a quarter to eight o’clock,” it said, “a gentleman who desires to consult you upon a matter of the very deepest moment. Your recent services to one of the royal houses of Europe have shown that you are one who may safely be trusted with matters which are of an importance which can hardly be exaggerated. This account of you we have from all quarters received. Be in your chamber then at that hour, and do not take it amiss if your visitor wear a mask.”
“This certainly is mysterious,” I said. “What do you suppose it can mean?”

“I have no evidence yet. Forming theories before you have evidence is a serious mistake. Without noticing it, you start bending the facts to fit your theories, instead of making your theories fit the facts. But look at the note itself. What can you infer from it?”
I studied the handwriting carefully, along with the paper on which it appeared.
“Presumably its author is comfortably off,” I said, trying to follow my companion's methods. “Paper like this must cost at least half a crown a packet. It is unusually strong and stiff.”
“Unusual—that is exactly the word,” Holmes said. “This paper is not English at all. Hold it against the light.”
I followed his instruction and saw, woven into the paper, a capital ‘E’ beside a small ‘g’, a ‘P’, and a capital ‘G’ beside a small ‘t’.
“What do you think that signifies?” Holmes asked.
“The name of its manufacturer, surely—or, more precisely, his monogram.”

“Not so. The ‘G’ and small ‘t’ abbreviate ‘Gesellschaft’, the German word for ‘Company’. It is a standard abbreviation, just like our ‘Co.’ Naturally, ‘P’ means ‘Papier’. That leaves ‘Eg’. Let us consult our Continental Gazetteer.” He lifted a heavy brown book from the shelves. “Eglow, Eglonitz—here it is: Egria. It lies in a German-speaking country—in Bohemia, near Carlsbad. ‘Remarkable as being the scene of the death of Wallenstein, and for its numerous glass-factories and paper-mills.’ Ha, ha, my boy! What do you say to that?” His eyes shone, and a great blue cloud rose triumphantly from his cigarette.
“So the paper was manufactured in Bohemia,” I said.

“Exactly. And a German wrote the note. Notice that oddly constructed sentence: ‘This account of you we have from all quarters received.’ No Frenchman or Russian would have written it. It takes a German to treat his verbs so discourteously. All we need to find out now is what this German wants—a man who uses Bohemian paper and would rather put on a mask than show his face. And unless I am mistaken, he has just arrived to settle all our doubts.”
As he finished, we heard the sharp clatter of horses' hooves and wheels scraping the kerb, followed by a vigorous tug at the bell. Holmes gave a whistle.

“Two horses, judging by the sound,” he said. “Yes,” he added, looking out of the window, “a fine little brougham, and a beautiful pair. A hundred and fifty guineas each. Whatever else this case may offer, Watson, it offers money.”
“Holmes, I think I ought to leave.”
“Certainly not, Doctor. Remain where you are. Without my Boswell I am lost. Besides, this looks promising. Missing it would be a shame.”
“But what about your client—”
“Don't concern yourself with him. I may need your assistance; he may too. Here he is. Take that armchair, Doctor, and listen as closely as you can.”
The slow, heavy footstep we had heard on the stairs and along the passage stopped just outside our door. A loud, commanding knock followed.
“Come in!” Holmes called.

The man who entered could scarcely have stood less than six feet six inches tall, and his chest and limbs were those of a Hercules. His clothes displayed a richness that in England would have approached bad taste. Broad, heavy strips of astrakhan crossed the sleeves and front of his double-breasted coat. Over his shoulders hung a deep-blue cloak lined with flame-coloured silk, fastened at his neck by a brooch made from a single fiery beryl. His boots reached halfway up his calves, their tops edged with rich brown fur, completing the impression of barbaric splendour given by his whole appearance. In one hand he held a broad-brimmed hat. A black vizard mask covered the upper part of his face and reached below his cheekbones. He seemed to have adjusted it only a moment before, for his other hand was still raised to it as he came in. The visible lower part of his face suggested a forceful character: a thick, drooping lip and a long, straight chin that spoke of determination carried to the point of obstinacy.
“You received my note?” he asked in a deep, rough voice, with a pronounced German accent. “I said I would come.” His gaze moved between us, as though he could not decide which man to address.
“Please sit down,” said Holmes. “My friend and colleague, Dr. Watson, is sometimes kind enough to assist me with my cases. May I ask whom I have the honour of addressing?”

“You may call me Count Von Kramm, a nobleman of Bohemia. I take it that your friend is an honourable, discreet gentleman, whom I can trust with a matter of the utmost importance. Otherwise I would much prefer to speak with you in private.”

I stood to leave, but Holmes seized my wrist and pressed me back into my seat. “You speak to both of us, or to neither,” he said. “Anything you can say to me may be said in this gentleman's presence.”

The Count's broad shoulders rose in a shrug. “In that case,” he said, “I must first require absolute secrecy from you both for two years. After that, the matter will no longer be important. At present, it is no exaggeration to say that its consequences could affect the history of Europe.”
“You have my promise,” said Holmes.
“And mine.”

“Forgive the mask,” our peculiar visitor went on. “The exalted personage I serve wishes his representative to remain unknown to you. I may admit immediately that the title I have just given you is not quite my own.”
“I had noticed,” Holmes replied drily.

“This is an extremely delicate situation. We must take every precaution to suppress something that could become a tremendous scandal, seriously compromising one of Europe's reigning families. To put it plainly, the matter concerns the great House of Ormstein, the hereditary kings of Bohemia.”
“That, too, I had noticed,” Holmes murmured, settling comfortably into his armchair and shutting his eyes.

Our visitor looked somewhat surprised by the languid figure reclining before him. No doubt Holmes had been described to him as Europe's sharpest reasoner and most energetic investigator. Slowly Holmes opened his eyes again and gave his enormous client an impatient look.
“If your Majesty would be so good as to explain your case,” he said, “I would be in a better position to advise you.”

The man leaped out of his chair and began striding up and down the room, unable to master his agitation. Then, in a desperate gesture, he ripped the mask off his face and flung it to the floor. “You are right!” he cried. “I am the King. Why should I try to hide it?”
“Why indeed?” Holmes said quietly. “Before your Majesty spoke a word, I knew I was addressing Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, Grand Duke of Cassel-Felstein and hereditary King of Bohemia.”

“But you must understand,” said our strange visitor, sitting again and running his hand across his high, pale forehead, “you must understand that I am not used to handling business of this sort myself. Yet it was too delicate to entrust to a representative without placing myself in his power. I have travelled from Prague _incognito_ to consult you.”
“Then please do so,” said Holmes, closing his eyes again.
“Briefly, these are the facts. About five years ago, while making an extended stay in Warsaw, I met the well-known adventuress Irene Adler. No doubt you know the name.”

“Doctor, would you look her up in my index?” Holmes murmured, his eyes still shut. For years he had kept a system of filing every paragraph he came across concerning people and subjects. It was difficult to name anything or anyone about whom he could not immediately supply information. This time I discovered her life history between those of a Hebrew rabbi and a staff-commander who had written a monograph on deep-sea fish.

“Let me see!” said Holmes. “Hum! Born in New Jersey, 1858. Contralto—hum! La Scala, hum! Prima donna at the Imperial Opera in Warsaw—yes! Retired from the operatic stage—ha! Residing in London—quite so! As I understand it, your Majesty became involved with this young person, sent her some compromising letters, and now wishes to recover them.”
“Exactly. But how did—”
“Did you marry in secret?”
“No.”
“Were there any legal documents or certificates?”
“None.”
“Then I do not understand your Majesty's difficulty. If this young person were to produce the letters for blackmail or any other purpose, how could she establish that they were genuine?”
“She has my handwriting.”
“Nonsense! It could be forged.”
“My personal writing paper.”
“It could be stolen.”
“My own seal.”
“It could be copied.”
“A photograph of me.”
“It could be purchased.”
“The photograph shows both of us together.”
“Oh dear! That is most unfortunate! Your Majesty has certainly acted indiscreetly.”
“I was mad—quite insane.”
“You have put yourself in a very compromising position.”
“At the time I was only Crown Prince. I was young. Even now I am only thirty.”
“We must get it back.”
“We have attempted that and failed.”
“Your Majesty will have to pay for it. You must buy it.”
“She refuses to sell it.”
“Then it must be stolen.”
“There have been five attempts. Burglars I hired have searched her house twice. On one journey we intercepted her luggage. Twice she has been stopped and searched. Nothing has come of it.”
“Not a trace of the photograph?”
“Not the slightest.”
Holmes gave a laugh. “A rather attractive little problem,” he said.
“But a very grave one for me,” the King replied reproachfully.
“Grave indeed. And what does she intend to do with this photograph?”
“She intends to ruin me.”
“In what way?”
“I am soon to marry.”
“Yes, I have heard as much.”

“Clotilde Lothman von Saxe-Meningen, the King of Scandinavia's second daughter. You may be familiar with her family's strict principles. She herself has the most delicate sense of propriety. The slightest suspicion about my behaviour would end the engagement.”
“And what of Irene Adler?”

“She threatens to send them the photograph. And she will. I know she will. You do not know her; her will is made of steel. She has the face of a supremely beautiful woman and the mind of a man of the utmost determination. There is nothing she would not do to keep me from marrying another woman—nothing.”
“Are you certain she has not already sent it?”
“I am quite certain.”
“On what grounds?”
“She said she would send it on the day our engagement was publicly announced. The announcement will be next Monday.”

“Then we still have three days,” said Holmes, yawning. “That is fortunate, since I have one or two important matters demanding my attention at the moment. Your Majesty will naturally remain in London for now?”
“Of course. I am staying at the Langham as Count Von Kramm.”
“I will send you a short note, then, to report our progress.”
“Please do. I shall be waiting most anxiously.”
“And now, what about the money?”
“You have _carte blanche_.”
“Without any limit?”
“I assure you, I would surrender a province of my kingdom to possess that photograph.”
“And to cover our immediate expenses?”
From beneath his cloak, the King produced a heavy bag of chamois leather and placed it on the table.
“You will find three hundred pounds in gold and seven hundred in banknotes,” he said.
Holmes hastily wrote a receipt on a page from his notebook and passed it to him.
“And where does Mademoiselle live?” he asked.
“At Briony Lodge, Serpentine Avenue, St. John's Wood.”
Holmes wrote the address down. “One further question,” he said. “Was it a cabinet photograph?”
“Yes, it was.”

“Then good night, your Majesty. I hope we shall soon be able to bring you good news. And good night to you, Watson,” he added as the royal brougham's wheels rolled away down the street. “If you could come here tomorrow afternoon at three, I would enjoy discussing this little affair with you.”

I reached Baker Street at precisely three o'clock, but Holmes was still out. His landlady told me he had left a little after eight that morning. Nevertheless, I settled beside the fire, determined to wait however long he took. The inquiry already interested me deeply. It had none of the grim and strange circumstances surrounding the two crimes I have previously recorded; even so, the nature of this case and the lofty position of his client gave it a distinctive character. Indeed, quite apart from the particular investigation occupying my friend, his masterful command of a situation and his sharp, penetrating reasoning always made it a pleasure to study his way of working. I enjoyed following the swift, subtle methods by which he unravelled apparently insoluble mysteries. I had grown so accustomed to his unfailing success that I no longer even considered the possibility of failure.

It was nearly four when the door opened and a groom came in: untidy, with side-whiskers, a flushed face, shabby clothes, and the appearance of being drunk. Familiar though I was with my friend's astonishing skill at disguise, I had to look three times before I felt certain it was Holmes. He nodded and disappeared into the bedroom. Five minutes later he emerged in tweeds, looking as respectable as ever. With his hands in his pockets and his legs stretched towards the fire, he laughed heartily for several minutes.
“Well, really!” he exclaimed, before choking with laughter again, until he had to sink back into his chair, limp and helpless.
“What has happened?”
“It is too ridiculous. You would never guess how I spent the morning, or what I ended up doing.”
“I cannot imagine. I suppose you have been observing Miss Irene Adler's habits, and perhaps keeping watch on her house.”

“Exactly; but what followed was unusual. Let me explain. I left a little after eight this morning, disguised as an unemployed groom. Men who work with horses share a remarkable fellow-feeling, a kind of freemasonry. Become one of them and you can learn everything there is to know. I soon located Briony Lodge. It is a _bijou_ villa, two storeys high, with a garden behind it and its front built right up to the road. The door has a Chubb lock. On the right is a large, well-furnished sitting-room, with tall windows reaching almost to the floor and those absurd English window catches that a child could open. There was nothing noteworthy at the back, except that one could reach the passage window from the coach-house roof. I walked around and inspected it carefully from every angle, but found nothing else of interest.

“Then I strolled down the street and, just as I expected, found a mews in a lane running beside one wall of the garden. I helped the stablemen rub down their horses. In return I got twopence, a glass of half-and-half, two pipefuls of shag tobacco, and all the information I could wish for about Miss Adler. I also had to listen to the life histories of half a dozen other local residents who did not interest me in the least.”
“What did you learn about Irene Adler?” I asked.

“Oh, every man in the district is besotted with her. According to all the men at Serpentine-mews, without exception, she is the loveliest creature who ever wore a bonnet. She leads a quiet life, sings in concerts, goes driving every day at five, and comes back for dinner at seven precisely. Apart from her singing, she seldom goes out at other times. She has just one male visitor, but sees a great deal of him. He is dark, handsome, and dashing, visits at least once a day, and often twice. His name is Mr. Godfrey Norton, of the Inner Temple. You see how useful it is to make a confidant of a cabman. They had driven him home from Serpentine-mews a dozen times and knew everything about him. Once I had heard all they could tell me, I returned to walking up and down near Briony Lodge, considering my plan of action.

“Clearly this Godfrey Norton mattered to the case. He was a lawyer, which sounded ominous. What was their relationship, and why did he call so often? Was she his client, his friend, or his mistress? If she was his client, she had probably entrusted the photograph to him. If his mistress, that seemed less likely. The answer would determine whether I should keep working at Briony Lodge or shift my attention to his chambers in the Temple. This was a delicate issue, and it broadened the scope of my investigation. I am afraid these details may bore you, but you must see the little difficulties I faced if you are to understand the situation.”
“I am listening very closely,” I replied.

“I was still weighing it up when a hansom pulled up at Briony Lodge and a gentleman jumped out. He was strikingly good-looking, dark, with an aquiline nose and a moustache—clearly the man they had described. He seemed terribly hurried. He shouted to the cabman to wait, then swept past the maid who answered the door with the confidence of someone entirely at home.

“He stayed about half an hour. Through the sitting-room windows I caught glimpses of him walking back and forth, speaking excitedly and waving his arms. I could see nothing of her. Eventually he came out, looking even more agitated. As he approached the cab, he drew a gold watch from his pocket and studied it closely. ‘Drive like the devil!’ he shouted. ‘First Gross & Hankey's in Regent Street, then St. Monica's Church in the Edgeware Road. Half a guinea if you get there in twenty minutes!’

“Off they went. I was considering whether I ought to follow when a tidy little landau appeared up the lane. Its coachman had his coat only half buttoned, his tie beneath his ear, and all the harness straps sticking out of their buckles. Before it had stopped, she darted out of the front door and into the carriage. I only glimpsed her then, but she was a lovely woman, with the kind of face a man might die for.
“‘St. Monica's Church, John!’ she called. ‘And half a sovereign if you get there in twenty minutes.’

“I could not let this opportunity escape, Watson. I was deciding whether to run after her or climb onto the back of her landau when a cab passed along the street. The driver looked twice at such a shabby passenger, but I was inside before he could protest. ‘St. Monica's Church,’ I said, ‘and half a sovereign if you get there in twenty minutes.’ It was twenty-five to twelve, and by then the purpose of all this was perfectly clear.

“My cabman drove fast. I doubt I have ever travelled faster, yet the others arrived before we did. When I got there, the cab and landau stood outside the church, their horses steaming. I paid my driver and hurried inside. The only people there were the pair I had followed and a clergyman in a surplice, who appeared to be arguing with them. All three stood together before the altar. I wandered along the side aisle like any idle visitor who had stepped into a church. Then, to my astonishment, all three turned towards me, and Godfrey Norton came running at full speed.
“‘Thank God!’ he cried. ‘You'll do! Come along! Come along!’
“‘What is the matter?’ I asked.
“‘Come on, man, come on! There are only three minutes left, or it won't be legal.’

“I was more or less dragged to the altar. Before I knew what was happening, I was mumbling replies whispered into my ear, attesting to matters I knew nothing about, and generally helping to join Irene Adler, spinster, securely in marriage to Godfrey Norton, bachelor. It was over in a moment. The gentleman thanked me on one side, the lady on the other, while the clergyman beamed at me from in front. I have never found myself in a more absurd position in my life. Remembering it was what set me laughing just now. Apparently there had been some irregularity in their licence, and the clergyman absolutely refused to perform the marriage without some kind of witness. My fortunate arrival spared the bridegroom a trip into the street to find himself a best man. The bride gave me a sovereign. I intend to hang it on my watch chain to commemorate the occasion.”
“That is a thoroughly unexpected development,” I said. “And what happened next?”

“Well, my plans were in considerable danger. The couple might leave immediately, which would force me to take swift and energetic action. At the church door, however, they parted: he drove back to the Temple, and she to her own house. ‘I shall go driving in the park at five as usual,’ she told him as they separated. That was all I heard. Their carriages went in opposite directions, and I left to make arrangements of my own.”
“What arrangements?”

“Cold beef and a glass of beer,” he replied, ringing the bell. “I have been too occupied to think about eating, and this evening promises to be busier still. Incidentally, Doctor, I shall need your assistance.”
“I would be delighted.”
“Would you object to breaking the law?”
“Not in the slightest.”
“Or taking the risk of being arrested?”
“Not for a worthy cause.”
“Oh, this cause is an excellent one!”
“In that case, count on me.”
“I knew I could depend on you.”
“But what do you need me to do?”

“Once Mrs. Turner brings the tray, I will explain everything. Now,” he said, turning hungrily to the plain meal our landlady had supplied, “I must talk while I eat, as time is short. It is almost five already. We must be at the scene in two hours. Miss Irene—or rather, Madame—comes back from her drive at seven. We have to meet her at Briony Lodge.”
“And what happens after that?”
“Leave that part to me. I have already arranged what will happen. There is just one thing I must insist upon. Whatever happens, you must not intervene. Is that clear?”
“I am to stay neutral?”

“You must do absolutely nothing. There will probably be a little unpleasantness. Keep out of it. It will result in my being carried into the house. Four or five minutes later, the sitting-room window will be opened. Take up a position close to that open window.”
“Yes.”
“Keep your eyes on me; you will be able to see me.”
“Yes.”
“When I lift my hand—like this—throw the thing I give you into the room, and at the same moment shout ‘Fire!’ Do you understand everything so far?”
“Perfectly.”

“It is nothing very alarming,” he said, drawing a long, cigar-shaped cylinder from his pocket. “Just a plumber's ordinary smoke-rocket, with a cap on each end so that it lights itself. That is all you have to do. When you shout ‘Fire!’, plenty of other people will take up the cry. Then walk to the end of the street, where I will join you ten minutes later. Have I explained it clearly?”
“I am to keep out of it, move close to the window, watch you, and throw this thing inside when you signal. Then I shout ‘Fire!’ and wait for you at the street corner.”
“Exactly.”
“Then you can depend on me entirely.”
“Excellent. I think it is nearly time for me to get ready for my next part.”

He went into his bedroom and came back a few minutes later as a kindly, simple-minded Nonconformist clergyman. Only Mr. John Hare could have matched the broad black hat, loose trousers, white tie, sympathetic smile, and general air of peering, benevolent curiosity. Holmes did more than change his clothes. His expression, his behaviour, even his very soul seemed to alter with each new character he adopted. When he chose to specialise in crime, the theatre lost an excellent actor, just as science lost a penetrating reasoner.

We left Baker Street at a quarter past six, and reached Serpentine Avenue at ten minutes to seven. Dusk had already fallen, and the lamps were just being lit as we walked back and forth outside Briony Lodge, waiting for its resident to return. The house looked exactly as I had imagined it from Holmes's brief description, but the surroundings were less secluded than I expected. Indeed, for a small street in a quiet neighbourhood, it was remarkably lively. Shabbily dressed men stood smoking and laughing at one corner; a scissors-grinder had his wheel there; two guardsmen were flirting with a nursemaid; and several smartly dressed young men wandered about with cigars in their mouths.

“You see,” Holmes remarked as we walked to and fro outside the house, “this marriage makes things rather simpler. The photograph is now a weapon that cuts both ways. She is probably as unwilling for Mr. Godfrey Norton to see it as our client is for his princess to do so. The question now is: where shall we find it?”
“Where indeed could it be?”

“She is very unlikely to keep it on her person. It is a cabinet photograph, too large to hide easily in a woman's clothes. She knows the King is capable of having her stopped and searched. He has already tried that twice. So we can reasonably assume that she does not carry it with her.”
“Then where is it?”

“With her banker or her lawyer: those are two possibilities. Yet I am inclined to reject both. Women are naturally secretive, and they prefer to hide things themselves. Why entrust it to anybody else? She could rely on her own safekeeping, but could not know what political or indirect pressure might be applied to a businessman. Besides, remember that she has decided to use it in a matter of days. It must be somewhere she can readily get hold of it. It must be in her own home.”
“But burglars have searched it twice.”
“Pshaw! They had no idea how to search.”
“Then how will you search for it?”
“I shall not search.”
“What will you do?”
“I shall make her show it to me.”
“Surely she will refuse.”
“She will have no choice. But I can hear wheels rumbling: her carriage is coming. Now follow my instructions exactly.”

As he spoke, the glow of a carriage's sidelights appeared around the bend in the avenue. A smart little landau rattled up to Briony Lodge. When it stopped, one of the idle men at the corner rushed over to open the door, hoping to earn a copper. Another idler, arriving with the same hope, elbowed him aside. A violent argument began. The two guardsmen made it worse by supporting one of the men, while the scissors-grinder championed the other just as heatedly. Someone struck a blow. In a moment the lady, who had stepped out of her carriage, stood surrounded by a small crowd of flushed, struggling men, hitting savagely at one another with fists and sticks. Holmes plunged into the crowd to protect her. Just as he reached her, however, he cried out and fell, blood streaming down his face. At once the guardsmen fled in one direction and the idlers in the other. Several better-dressed onlookers, who had watched without joining the fight, now pressed forward to help the lady and attend to the injured man. Irene Adler, as I shall continue to call her, had hurried up the steps. She stood at the top, her splendid figure silhouetted against the light in the hall, looking back towards the street.
“Is the poor gentleman badly injured?” she asked.
“He's dead!” several voices cried out.
“No, no, he's still alive!” someone else shouted. “But he'll die before you can get him to a hospital.”
“He's a brave man,” a woman said. “Without him they'd have stolen the lady's watch and purse. They were a gang—a nasty, rough lot too. Ah, he's breathing again now.”
“We can't leave him in the street. May we carry him inside, ma'am?”
“Of course. Take him into the sitting-room. There is a comfortable sofa there. This way, please!”

They carried him slowly and solemnly into Briony Lodge and stretched him out in the main room. I continued watching from my position by the window. The lamps were alight, but the blinds remained open, giving me a clear view of Holmes on the couch. I cannot say whether he felt any remorse just then about the part he was playing. But I had never in my life felt more deeply ashamed of myself than I did at the sight of the beautiful woman against whom I was plotting, and the grace and kindness with which she cared for the injured man. Yet abandoning the role Holmes had entrusted to me now would have been the worst betrayal. I hardened my heart and drew the smoke-rocket from beneath my ulster. After all, I told myself, we were doing her no harm. We were merely stopping her from harming someone else.

Holmes sat up on the couch, and I saw him gesture like a man struggling for air. A maid hurried across and opened the window wide. At that instant he raised his hand. On his signal I threw the rocket inside and shouted ‘Fire!’ Scarcely had I spoken when the entire gathering, smartly dressed and shabby alike—gentlemen, stablemen, and servant girls—joined in a great cry of ‘Fire!’ Dense clouds of smoke curled around the room and out through the open window. I glimpsed people rushing about, then heard Holmes's voice from inside, reassuring them that the alarm was false. I slipped through the shouting crowd and made my way to the street corner. Ten minutes later I was delighted to feel my friend's arm through mine and to leave the uproar behind. He walked quickly and silently for several minutes, until we turned into one of the quiet streets leading towards the Edgeware Road.
“You carried that off splendidly, Doctor,” he said. “It could not have gone better. Everything is in order.”
“Have you got the photograph?”
“I have discovered where it is.”
“And how did you discover that?”
“She showed it to me, exactly as I said she would.”
“I still do not understand.”

“I have no wish to be mysterious,” he said with a laugh. “It was all quite straightforward. Naturally, you realised that everyone in the street was working with me. I had hired them all for the evening.”
“That was what I suspected.”
“When the fight began, I had a little wet red paint in my palm. I ran forward, fell, pressed my hand to my face, and became a pitiful sight. It is a familiar old trick.”
“I had worked that out as well.”

“Then they carried me inside. She had to let them bring me in—what else could she do? And they took me to her sitting-room, precisely the room I suspected. It had to be there or in her bedroom, and I meant to establish which. They put me on a couch; I signalled that I needed air; they had to open the window; and that gave you your opportunity.”
“But how did it help your investigation?”

“It was crucial. When a woman believes her house is burning, her first instinct is to run straight to whatever she values most. The impulse is overwhelming, and I have used it more than once. It served me in the Darlington Substitution Scandal, and in the Arnsworth Castle affair too. A married woman seizes her baby; an unmarried woman reaches for her jewel-box. It was clear to me that the lady in this case had nothing in the house she valued more than the object of our search. She would hurry to save it. The fire alarm was beautifully managed. That smoke and shouting could have shaken nerves of steel. Her response was everything I wanted. The photograph is hidden in a recess behind a sliding panel, just above the right-hand bell-pull. She reached it in an instant, and I glimpsed the photograph as she drew it halfway out. When I called that the alarm was false, she put it back, looked at the rocket, and hurried out of the room. I have not seen her since. I got up, made my excuses, and left the house. I considered taking the photograph immediately, but the coachman had come in and was watching me closely. Waiting seemed safer. A little excessive haste can spoil everything.”
“And what happens now?” I asked.

“Our search is almost over. Tomorrow I shall come back with the King—and with you, if you wish to join us. They will show us into the sitting-room to wait for her. By the time she arrives, she will probably find that both we and the photograph have gone. His Majesty might enjoy recovering it with his own hands.”
“What time will you go there?”

“Eight in the morning. She will still be in bed, leaving us free to act. Besides, we must be quick: this marriage could completely alter her life and habits. I must send the King a telegram immediately.”
We had arrived in Baker Street and stopped outside the door. While Holmes searched his pockets for his key, a passer-by said:
“Good-night, Mister Sherlock Holmes.”
Several people were on the pavement, but the greeting seemed to come from a slender young man in an ulster who had hurried past.
“I know that voice,” Holmes said, peering down the poorly lit street. “Who the devil could that have been, I wonder?”
I stayed the night at Baker Street. The next morning, while we were having our coffee and toast, the King of Bohemia burst into the room.
“You really have it!” he cried, taking Holmes by both shoulders and gazing eagerly into his face.
“Not as yet.”
“But you are hopeful?”
“Yes, I am hopeful.”
“Then let us go. I cannot bear to wait any longer.”
“We will need a cab.”
“No need; my brougham is outside.”
“That makes things easier, then.” We went downstairs and set out for Briony Lodge once again.
“Irene Adler has married,” Holmes observed.
“Married! When did that happen?”
“Yesterday.”
“But whom has she married?”
“An English lawyer by the name of Norton.”
“But she cannot possibly love him.”
“I am hoping that she does.”
“Why should you hope that?”

“Because your Majesty would then have nothing to fear from her in future. If she loves her husband, she does not love your Majesty. If she does not love your Majesty, she has no reason to obstruct your Majesty's plans.”
“That is true. And yet—! Well! If only she had belonged to my own rank! What a queen she could have been!” He fell into a brooding silence, which lasted until we stopped in Serpentine Avenue.
Briony Lodge's door stood open. An elderly woman on the steps watched us with a sardonic expression as we climbed out of the brougham.
“Mr. Sherlock Holmes, if I am not mistaken?” she said.
“Yes, I am Mr. Holmes,” my companion replied, giving her a questioning, slightly startled look.
“Indeed! My mistress said you would probably come. She and her husband left for the Continent this morning on the 5:15 train from Charing Cross.”
“What!” Holmes reeled back, pale with dismay and astonishment. “Are you telling me that she has left England?”
“And will never return.”
“What about the papers?” the King asked hoarsely. “Everything is lost.”

“We shall see about that.” Holmes brushed past the servant and hurried into the drawing-room, with the King and me following. Furniture stood scattered everywhere, shelves had been dismantled, and drawers lay open, as though she had hastily searched them before escaping. Holmes ran to the bell-pull, wrenched back a little sliding panel, thrust his hand inside, and brought out a letter and a photograph. The photograph showed Irene Adler alone, in evening dress. The letter was addressed: ‘Sherlock Holmes, Esq. To be left till called for.’ My friend tore it open, and the three of us read it together. Dated midnight the previous night, it said:

“MY DEAR MR. SHERLOCK HOLMES,—You carried it off remarkably well. I was completely deceived. Until the fire alarm was over, I suspected nothing. Then, realising how I had given myself away, I began to think. Months ago I was warned about you. I was told that if the King hired an agent, he would certainly choose you, and I was given your address. Despite all that, you made me disclose exactly what you wished to know. Even once I grew suspicious, it was difficult to imagine anything wicked of such a dear, kindly old clergyman. But I, too, have trained as an actress, you know. Dressing as a man is nothing new to me; I frequently enjoy the freedom it allows. I sent John, the coachman, to watch you, hurried upstairs, put on what I call my walking clothes, and returned downstairs just as you were leaving.

“I followed you to your own door. That confirmed that the celebrated Mr. Sherlock Holmes was indeed taking an interest in me. Rather rashly, I then wished you good night and went off to the Temple to see my husband.

“We agreed that flight was the best course when facing so formidable an opponent. When you call tomorrow, therefore, you will find an empty nest. Your client need have no anxiety about the photograph. I love a man better than he is, and that man loves me. The King may do as he pleases, unopposed by the woman he has treated so cruelly. I retain the photograph solely for my own protection, as a weapon that will always guard me against any action he might take in future. I am leaving another photograph that he may wish to keep. I remain, dear Mr. Sherlock Holmes,
“Very truly yours,
“IRENE NORTON, _née_ ADLER.”

“What a woman—oh, what a woman!” exclaimed the King of Bohemia after we had all read the letter. “Did I not say how resourceful and determined she was? Would she not have been a splendid queen? Is it not a pity that she was not on my level?”

“From what I have observed of her, she does indeed appear to stand on a very different level from your Majesty,” Holmes said coldly. “I regret that I have not been able to conclude your Majesty's business more successfully.”
“Quite the reverse, my dear sir!” the King cried. “It could not have ended better. I know she will never break her word. The photograph is now as harmless as if it had been burned.”
“I am pleased to hear your Majesty thinks so.”
“I owe you an enormous debt. Please tell me how I may reward you. This ring—” He took an emerald snake ring off his finger and offered it on his open palm.
“There is something your Majesty possesses that I would prize still more,” said Holmes.
“You need only say what it is.”
“This photograph!”
The King looked at him, utterly astonished.
“Irene's photograph!” he exclaimed. “Of course, if you would like it.”

“I thank your Majesty. There is nothing further for us to do in this matter. I have the honour of wishing you a very good morning.” He bowed, then turned away without seeming to notice the hand the King had held out to him, and set off with me for his rooms.

That, then, was how a great scandal threatened the kingdom of Bohemia, and how a woman's intelligence defeated Mr. Sherlock Holmes's most carefully laid plans. He once enjoyed making jokes about women's cleverness, but I have not heard him do so lately. Whenever he speaks of Irene Adler, or mentions her photograph, he gives her that same title of honour: _the_ woman.
